definition: Taste transduction is the process by which taste cells convert chemicals such as nicotine or ethanol into cellular signals. In this packet, it is described as involving receptors in taste cells that trigger temporary rises in internal calcium and can alter neurohumoral peptide release.

reasons: The packet supports that nicotine/ethanol exposure in (cultured) taste cells can produce transient increases in internal calcium ([Ca2+]i) and can change release of BDNF, but it does not describe BDNF as a “neurohumoral peptide,” so that part of the definition is not supported by the packet.

Because the definition states “can alter neurohumoral peptide release,” and the packet only mentions BDNF detection/release without using that neurohumoral-peptide framing, the definition includes an unsupported characterization.

The packet supports nicotine and ethanol effects in cultured human taste cells, but it does not support the broader generalization that taste transduction is generally the process by which taste cells convert chemicals into cellular signals.

The packet shows transient increases in intracellular calcium and nicotine-induced BDNF release, but it does not clearly support the definition’s claim that taste transduction involves altering neurohumoral peptide release.
“Neurohumoral peptide” is not established in the packet as the specific released substance; the packet names BDNF, which is not the same claim.
